blocks.text: BERTScore addresses the core weakness shared by BLEU and ROUGE, both covered in earlier topics, their inability to credit valid paraphrases, by comparing candidate and reference text using contextual embeddings from a pretrained language model instead of exact word overlap.

This topic covers how BERTScore actually computes similarity at the token level, why that catches paraphrases the earlier n-gram metrics miss, and what tradeoffs come with using a learned model as part of the evaluation itself.
1. Moving Past Surface Word Overlap
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472392111-537353659.png

BLEU and ROUGE, both covered in earlier topics, only credit exact matching word sequences, BERTScore instead measures how semantically similar candidate and reference text are, using representations that capture meaning rather than literal wording.
2. Contextual Embeddings as the Foundation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472392384-779419999.png

BERTScore passes both the candidate and reference text through a pretrained language model, producing a contextual embedding for every token, a vector representation that reflects not just the word itself but its meaning given the surrounding context, the same kind of representation covered in the earlier Embeddings related topics from the RAG course.
3. Token-Level Cosine Similarity
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472392386-746514313.png

For each pair of candidate and reference tokens, BERTScore computes cosine similarity between their embeddings, a value close to one meaning the tokens are semantically very close even if they are literally different words.
4. Greedy Matching Between Candidate and Reference

blocks.alt: Greedy Matching Between Candidate and Reference
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472392386-679226498.png

Rather than requiring tokens to align in a fixed order the way n-gram matching does, BERTScore greedily matches each candidate token to whichever reference token it is most similar to, then averages these best-match similarity scores into precision, recall, and F1 style figures analogous to how BLEU and ROUGE report their scores.

blocks.text: 5. Why BERTScore Catches Paraphrases
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472392387-610677786.png

Because BERTScore compares meaning rather than literal words, a candidate that says the same thing as the reference using entirely different phrasing scores well, directly addressing the paraphrase weakness that both BLEU and ROUGE, covered in earlier topics, share.

blocks.title: This is the main reason BERTScore gained adoption
blocks.content: Teams evaluating open ended generation tasks, where many different phrasings are equally valid, found BERTScore correlated much better with human judgment than the older n-gram overlap metrics did.

blocks.text: 6. The Compute Cost Tradeoff
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472392388-607258519.png

BERTScore requires running a language model forward pass over both candidate and reference text, a meaningfully higher compute cost than the simple counting BLEU and ROUGE, both covered in earlier topics, use, a real consideration when evaluating a very large number of examples repeatedly during training.
7. Choosing the Underlying Model

BERTScore quality depends on which pretrained model produces the embeddings, a stronger, more capable underlying model generally produces embeddings that better capture nuanced meaning, but also increases the compute cost of running the metric, a tradeoff worth tuning based on how the score will be used.
8. BERTScore Is Still an Automated Proxy

blocks.alt: BERTScore Is Still an Automated Proxy
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472392388-6743077.png

Despite being a meaningful improvement over BLEU and ROUGE, BERTScore is still an automated approximation, it can still be fooled by text that is semantically similar but factually wrong, or miss subtle quality differences a human reviewer would immediately notice, the same fundamental limitation every automated metric in this module shares.
9. Where BERTScore Fits in an Evaluation Pipeline

BERTScore works well as a middle ground between cheap n-gram metrics and expensive human evaluation, covered in an earlier topic, useful for tracking semantic quality across many training checkpoints at a compute cost still far below running full human review on every checkpoint.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a paraphrasing model finds that BLEU scores stay disappointingly low even as the model outputs look genuinely good on manual inspection, since correct paraphrases by definition avoid reusing the reference exact wording.

Switching to BERTScore for the same checkpoints shows a much clearer, steadily rising trend that tracks the model actual improving quality far more closely, letting the team use an automated metric during rapid iteration instead of needing a human reviewer for every checkpoint.
Common Mistakes

items: Choosing BLEU or ROUGE for a task like paraphrasing where the reference wording is intentionally not reused
Assuming a high BERTScore guarantees factual correctness, when it only measures semantic similarity
Ignoring the added compute cost when running BERTScore on very large evaluation sets repeatedly during training
Comparing BERTScore results computed with different underlying pretrained models as if they were directly comparable

blocks.text: Practice

Take a reference sentence and write a candidate that says the same thing using completely different words, then reason through how BLEU, ROUGE, and BERTScore would likely score that candidate differently, and why BERTScore is designed to handle this case better.
Key Takeaway

BERTScore compares candidate and reference text using contextual embeddings and cosine similarity rather than exact word overlap, directly addressing the paraphrase blindness that BLEU and ROUGE both share, at the cost of extra compute, making it a strong middle ground metric for evaluating open ended generation quality during fine-tuning.
